turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's a pleasure to meet you. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. Well, I guess what brings me in is that... I just feel like I’m constantly running on a motor lately. 

Like, I teach special education, and the kids really keep you on your toes, which I love. Actually, just this morning one of my boys brought in this enormous collection of vintage Matchbox cars—fascinating stuff, really. I used to collect the die-cast ones when I was his age, the ones with the little opening doors? I had this bright orange Mustang that I took everywhere until the wheels literally fell off. I think my mother eventually threw it out when I went off to college, which is a shame because they're worth a bit of money now on eBay... 

But anyway, sorry, what I mean is... I'll finish one thing at school, or even at home, and I just immediately jump right into the next project. I never stop. I get home from teaching and I'm instantly cleaning out the garage, and then halfway through that I'm fixing the fence. It's like I've completely lost the ability to just sit down and shut myself off.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts, going on a tangent about Matchbox cars before catching themselves and returning to the topic.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly states feeling like they are 'constantly running on a motor' and have lost the ability to sit down and shut off.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient describes a recent increase in goal-directed activity and energy, such as immediately jumping into cleaning the garage and fixing the fence after a full day of teaching.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: During these times when you feel like you're running on a motor, do you also feel unusually high-spirited, euphoric, or irritable, or is it more of a persistent sense of restlessness?
turns.patient_response:
Euphoric? No, no, definitely not. I wouldn't say I'm unusually high-spirited or angry or anything like that. It's really just... I just have this constant itch to be moving. Like I have to be doing *something* at all times. 

Actually, I was doing some landscaping last weekend because I just couldn't sit still to watch the football game on TV. I decided to pull up all these old azalea bushes out front instead. Azaleas are incredibly stubborn, you know. The root systems on those things just go on forever, they really dig in. My neighbor, Tom, he saw me struggling and came over to help, and he actually brought his truck around to try and pull the stumps out with a chain. We ended up snapping the tow strap right in half! Sounded exactly like a gunshot. His wife came running out onto the porch in her slippers, holding a spatula because she was right in the middle of making pancakes... Oh, man, they make the absolute best blueberry pancakes, they use the wild blueberries they pick up in Maine every summer. 

But, uh... I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the moods. Yeah, no, I'm just regular old me, just... very restless, I guess.

symptom_reasoning.S008: Patient gets distracted by his own tangential thoughts about landscaping and pancakes, losing track of the doctor's original question.
symptom_reasoning.S012: Patient explicitly states he is 'very restless' and has a 'constant itch to be moving.'
symptom_reasoning.S013: Patient mentions he 'couldn't sit still to watch the football game on TV,' indicating difficulty engaging in leisure activities quietly.
symptom_reasoning.S014: Patient describes feeling like he has to be 'doing something at all times.'
symptom_reasoning.S033: Patient explicitly denies feeling euphoric, unusually high-spirited, or angry.

turns.doctor_question: When you are jumping between these different tasks, do you find it difficult to focus on one thing at a time because your mind keeps drifting to other topics?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's not really that my mind is drifting, exactly. It's more like... I just see something else that needs doing, and I have to go do it right then. 

Like with the garage. I was in there to get a rake for the yard, right? And I saw the box of old Christmas ornaments sitting on the wrong shelf. The shelf was bowing a little, actually. It's one of those cheap particle board things I put up maybe fifteen years ago. You know, you buy them at the hardware store and think they'll last forever, but the humidity just ruins them. We had a really bad leak in the roof a few years back, right over the garage, and the water just soaked into everything. I had to replace a whole section of drywall myself. Drywalling is a terrible job, by the way, all that dust gets everywhere. You breathe it in for days no matter how good your mask is...

But anyway, I saw the ornaments, so I started moving them, and then I realized the whole shelf needed to come down. So I went to get my drill, but the battery was dead, so I put it on the charger, and while I was waiting for that, I noticed the hinges on the back door were squeaking... 

So, I don't know if that's my mind drifting. I'm just... doing things. I just can't seem to just do the one thing I started out to do.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient admits they 'can't seem to just do the one thing I started out to do,' illustrating a failure to finish the initial chore (getting a rake).
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous visual and auditory stimuli, such as seeing a box of ornaments or noticing squeaky hinges.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, going on a long, unprompted tangent about particle board, roof leaks, and drywalling before returning to the point.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your childhood or your time in school, did you experience this same level of restlessness and difficulty staying on one task?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. This isn't a new thing at all. It's been this way for as long as I can remember, long before any recent family changes or whatever. My mother, actually, she used to joke that even back in elementary school, I was basically teaching the class from my seat. 

Well, not from my seat, really, because I was never in it! I was always out of my chair, pacing around, talking to the other kids. The poor teachers... I was always cutting in before they even finished giving directions. I just had to get the thought out, you know? Like this one time in fourth grade, Mrs. Gable's class. She was trying to explain how to make these papier-mâché volcanoes for the science fair. Have you ever made one of those? You mix the flour and water, and it gets everywhere. It's like cement if you let it dry on the desk. My mom had given me one of my dad's old button-down shirts to wear backwards as a smock. It was this hideous plaid thing from the seventies, mustard yellow and brown. I think dad bought it for a golf trip to Myrtle Beach, but he never wore it again because he spilled cocktail sauce all down the front of it at a seafood buffet...

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the volcano. Yeah, Mrs. Gable was trying to explain the baking soda and vinegar part, and I just kept blurting out the chemical reaction before she could finish. I just couldn't hold it in. So yeah, this restlessness, it's just always been part of who I am.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by unrelated thoughts about a plaid shirt and a golf trip, losing their train of thought mid-sentence.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they were 'never in' their seat and 'always out of my chair' during class.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms experiencing 'restlessness' that has always been a part of who they are.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient describes 'blurting out the chemical reaction before she could finish' in class.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient mentions 'cutting in before they even finished giving directions,' indicating a habit of interrupting others.

turns.doctor_question: In your daily life, do you find that you frequently lose or misplace things you need for your tasks, like your keys, phone, or tools?
turns.patient_response:
Lose things? No, not really. I mean, I don't think I misplace things any more than the average guy. I've got my system, you know? Keys go in the bowl by the door. Always. 

Well, except for last Tuesday. I was coming in the door with groceries, and one of the bags ripped. It was the paper ones, you know? They always ask "paper or plastic" at the store, and I try to do the right thing for the environment, so I say paper. But they overload them! They put the milk jug right in with the canned goods. Who does that? It's just asking for a blowout. So, the bag rips right on the porch, and the cans of soup go rolling everywhere. I had bought this minestrone, my wife loves minestrone, but only the kind with the little shell pasta, not the macaroni. If you get the macaroni, she won't eat it. Says it gets too mushy. Which I guess is true, nobody likes mushy pasta. 

Anyway, I was trying to catch the cans before they rolled off the porch into the bushes—those same azalea bushes I was telling you about—and I must have set my keys down on the porch railing. Spent twenty minutes looking for them the next morning before I found them sitting right there next to a potted geranium. 

But generally speaking? No, I don't really lose things that often. I keep track of my stuff pretty well.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a long, rambling, and overly detailed story about grocery bags, soup, and pasta shapes to answer a simple question, demonstrating excessive talking.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly denies frequently losing or misplacing things, stating he has a system and keeps track of his stuff well.

turns.doctor_question: When you are in social or work settings, do you find that you often interrupt others while they are speaking or find it difficult to wait for your turn in conversation?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, definitely. I mean, I don't do it to be rude, I just... I get so eager to help out or solve the problem. Like at school, I'm a special education teacher, you know, and we have these IEP meetings with the parents and the other staff. And someone will be explaining a situation, maybe the speech therapist or the principal, and I just know exactly what they're going to say, or I know the solution right away. So I just jump right in. 

I do it with my wife, too. Like last weekend, her sister was visiting. Her sister lives down in Florida, near Tampa. Actually, it's closer to Clearwater, right near the beach. They get terrible hurricanes down there, though. I keep telling them they should move further inland, but she loves the ocean. She collects these little seashells, the really tiny ones, and she glues them onto picture frames. She sells them at craft fairs. It's actually a pretty good little side business for her, she makes enough to cover her car payment every month. She drives this little blue Honda, great gas mileage... 

But anyway, she and my wife were talking about their mom's upcoming birthday, trying to figure out what to do for a party, and I just kept jumping into the conversation. I had all these ideas for a venue and the catering, and I just kind of took charge before they even finished figuring out the guest list. My wife had to actually put her hand on my arm and tell me to let her sister finish a sentence. I just get so wrapped up in trying to help, I end up talking right over people.

symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient explicitly agrees ('Oh, definitely') to the doctor's question about finding it difficult to wait their turn in conversation.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient admits to frequently jumping into conversations, taking charge, and talking right over people before they can finish.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient demonstrates tangential speech by wandering off-topic into a long, unrelated story about their sister-in-law's location, hurricanes, seashell crafts, and car before returning to the main point.

turns.doctor_question: When you are working on your various tasks, do you often find that you make careless mistakes because you are rushing or have difficulty sustaining your attention on the details of the work itself?
turns.patient_response:
Careless mistakes? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I'm pretty thorough when it comes to the details. Especially with the IEPs—you have to be, right? Those documents are legally binding. You can't just slap them together. 

Though, I will say, the new software the district makes us use is a nightmare. It's called SpedTrack or something like that, and it's supposed to make everything streamlined, but it just takes twice as long. You have to click through five different screens just to update a goal. And the font is so small! I told the IT guy, Gary—nice guy, always wears these novelty ties, last week he had one with little cartoon tacos all over it. I asked him where he gets them, and he said his daughter buys them for him for Father's Day every year. She's at college now, up in Maine. Bowdoin, I think? Or maybe Bates. One of those small liberal arts schools where it snows eight months out of the year. I could never live in Maine. I hate shoveling. I bought a snowblower three years ago, a Toro, two-stage. Best investment I ever made. It cuts through the heavy, wet stuff at the end of the driveway like butter. The city plows always push it right back into your driveway after you've cleared it, you know? It's infuriating. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Mistakes at work? No, I don't really make careless mistakes. I'm pretty careful about all that.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly denies making careless mistakes, stating they are thorough and careful with details.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides an excessively long, rambling response to a simple question.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from work software to an IT guy's ties, his daughter, snowblowers, and eventually forgetting the original question.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find that you have trouble organizing your tasks or managing your time when you have a lot of things to get done?
turns.patient_response:
Organizing tasks? Time management? No, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I have trouble with it. I've got a pretty good handle on my schedule. You have to, in my line of work. Between the classroom, the meetings, the paperwork... you just have to stay on top of it. 

I usually make a list every morning while I'm having my coffee. I drink this dark roast, French roast, actually. I get the beans whole and grind them myself. You really can taste the difference when you grind them fresh. My wife bought me this burr grinder for Christmas a couple of years ago. The blade ones just chop the beans up unevenly, but the burr grinder crushes them, so you get a consistent size. It makes a huge difference in the extraction. We get our beans from this little local roaster downtown. The guy who owns it, Marco, he used to be a stockbroker in Chicago, but he gave it all up to roast coffee. Said the stress was killing him. I can imagine. Chicago winters are brutal, too. The wind coming off the lake... it just cuts right through you. I went there once for a conference, stayed right on the Magnificent Mile. Ate at this deep-dish pizza place. It was good, but honestly, it's more like a casserole than a pizza, you know? You have to eat it with a knife and fork. I'm more of a thin-crust guy myself. Fold it in half, New York style. 

But yeah, organizing? No, I don't think I have any real trouble with that. I just make my lists and get things done.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, going on a long, unprompted tangent about coffee, grinders, Chicago, and pizza before finally returning to the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly denies having trouble organizing tasks or managing time, noting that they make daily lists and have a good handle on their schedule.

turns.doctor_question: Beyond your tendency to jump into conversations, would you say that your most significant and persistent struggle is this internal and physical need to be constantly moving and active?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I guess you could say that. It's actually the main reason I'm here. I just feel like I'm constantly running on a motor lately. Like, I finish one thing at school, or even at home, and I immediately have to jump into the next thing. I just can't seem to shut myself off. It's exhausting. 

My wife keeps telling me I need to learn how to relax. She bought me this hammock for the backyard, one of those nice woven ones from South America. Ecuador, I think. Or maybe Colombia. The tag said it was fair trade, which is important to her. She volunteers at this co-op downtown that sells all sorts of fair trade goods. Baskets, jewelry, coffee... actually, they sell a really good shade-grown Guatemalan roast there. But anyway, she set up the hammock between the two big oak trees in our backyard. We have these massive oaks, probably a hundred years old. The acorns in the fall are a nightmare, though. I have to rake them up every weekend or the lawnmower turns them into shrapnel. I broke a window on the garage two years ago because a rock or an acorn or something shot out from under the mower deck. Shattered the whole pane. I had to go down to the hardware store and buy a piece of plexiglass to fix it. The guy at the hardware store, old guy named Frank, he's been working there since the seventies. He knows where every single screw and nail is in that place. It's amazing. 

But yeah, I try to lie in the hammock, and I just... I can't. I'm there for two minutes, and I'm already thinking about cleaning the gutters or reorganizing the garage. I just can't stop moving.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, as their mind wanders from a hammock to fair trade goods, coffee, acorns, and a hardware store.
symptom_reasoning.S013: The patient describes an inability to engage in a relaxing leisure activity (lying in a hammock), stating they can only last two minutes before needing to do chores.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly confirms the symptom, stating they feel like they are 'constantly running on a motor' and 'can't stop moving.'
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, providing a long, rambling, and unnecessarily detailed story in response to the doctor's question.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality, wandering far off-topic through a chain of loosely related associations before finally returning to the original point.
